claims.text: The initially solid Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles are single-phase homogeneous solid solutions.
Localized surface segregation initiates premelting in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
Differential elemental mobilities drive the proposed surface segregation.
Minor local compositional fluctuations reduce the local energy barrier for surface melting.
Copper is a lower-melting-point constituent of the Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu particle.
Local copper enrichment triggers an incipient liquid phase before homogeneous melting.
Heating induces differential surface diffusion among the constituent elements.
Differential surface diffusion causes copper and other lower-melting constituents to accumulate at the particle surface.
Surface enrichment in lower-melting constituents lowers the local melting temperature.
The locally reduced melting temperature nucleates a premelted surface layer.
The premelted surface layer provides a pathway for subsequent overall melting.
Five-element nanoparticle formation under limited atomic mobility can yield a substantially mixed particle while retaining signs of local segregation.
In situ TEM can monitor nanoscale kinetic and structural changes at high spatial resolution.
A thin liquid-like surface layer will appear below the homogeneous melting temperature.
The liquid-like surface layer will spatially coincide with regions enriched in lower-melting-point constituents relative to the core.
Compositionally uniform or simpler baseline nanoparticles lacking pronounced segregation will melt more uniformly and at a higher temperature.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to larger particles or to particles synthesized under conditions affording high atomic mobility.
The extent and kinetics of surface segregation depend on particle size, heating rate, and synthesis history.
The absence of significant surface compositional gradients together with homogeneous melting would falsify the proposed segregation-controlled premelting mechanism.
